summary:
I've been leaning on Claude to build a Japanese-learning dashboard for myself, keikochō, from scratch — placement tests, spaced drills, dialogue practice, the whole loop. The interesting constraint is that I'm a true beginner: no kanji, still working through hiragana. Early on I tried a typed-input placement test and watched myself stall three items in, because typing romaji asks for production skill I don't have yet. Swapped it for four-tile selection with audio on every option, and engagement picked right back up. Same principle now runs everything: recognition before production, always an audio button, never a free-text field for anything I haven't actually mastered.

The dialogue drill (会話) is where the design got more interesting than "flashcards." Exchanges like "where's the station?" / "the station is here" get broken into listen/reply/build/say items, and the sentence-builder mode deliberately allows promotion past the early boxes — a departure from the matching-game rule elsewhere — because there's no way to guess the right word order with a ~1% floor. I also had to walk back a plan to loosen a readability gate (every drill unit needs at least three known pieces) once I actually checked live data and realized the block was one specific dakuten sound away, not a design flaw.

On the character-creation side (SillyTavern extensions), I did a competitive survey before writing more code — turned up one clear incumbent at 157 stars and a much smaller project that had, independently, converged on the same phased design I was already building: guided stages, staged drafts requiring approval, a persistent brief across turns. Confirming that a five-star repo landed on the same architecture from scratch was a better signal than any amount of my own confidence would have been.

I also spent a chunk of time on a debugging problem that turned out to be an infrastructure lesson more than a code one: a shared GPU broker was silently corrupting file paths and identifiers in long agentic runs, and the fix that actually held wasn't a sampler tweak, it was keeping exact filenames out of the model's tool calls in the first place. A good reminder that the "smart" fix isn't always the one that survives contact with a flaky component.

highlights.oneLiner: Traced GPU-broker corruption to model-visible filenames, not the sampler; fixed by keeping them out of tool calls.
